items.title: Eight nebulae as walls of glowing gas, dust and stars
items.summary: Release 1.4.0 draws the Lagoon, Trifid, Eagle, Omega, Rosette and three more nebulae in 3D. The light is measured, the shape reconstructed.

items.title: New Horizons at Pluto: When Was Closest Approach, and How Close?
items.summary: When was New Horizons’ closest approach to Pluto? 14 July 2015, about 12,500 km up at 13.8 km/s. The two clocks, Charon, and what a replay reconstructs.

items.title: Curiosity’s Landing: The Seven Minutes of Terror, Step by Step
items.summary: Why is Curiosity’s landing called the seven minutes of terror? The JPL clock, NASA’s heights and speeds, the sky crane, and what a replay must reconstruct.

items.title: Stars with no distance, 4 383 pulsars and the farthest galaxy
items.summary: Release 1.5.0 adds 10 224 stars with no measured distance, 4 383 pulsars, the Local Group's dwarfs, quasars and MoM-z14 at redshift 14.44.

items.title: Arrokoth, Kleopatra and nine more small worlds in their own shapes
items.summary: Release 1.5.0 draws eleven asteroids and a comet from the shape models of New Horizons, Lucy, Rosetta and radar, each on its own orbit.

items.title: Moments: a mission replayed in 3D on one clock
items.summary: Release 1.5.0 adds Moments, missions replayed in 3D on one clock. The first is Apollo 11's Saturn V from ignition to the escape tower.

items.title: Free planetarium software for a classroom with no Wi-Fi
items.summary: Free planetarium software that runs with no internet: how a school keeps its own copy of Space Radar, what a lesson looks like, and what stops working.

items.title: A solar eclipse simulator, and a clock you can drag
items.summary: A solar eclipse simulator is a clock you can drag. What obeys when you scrub time on Space Radar's live map of space, what does not, and why it says so.

items.title: A virtual space tour that begins with a family photo
items.summary: A virtual space tour should be a story, not a manual. How Space Radar's 26 narrated trips are written, and three retold, from the Moon to a dead star.

items.title: What Is in the Sky Tonight? Relearning to Look Up
items.summary: Most of us have never seen the Milky Way from home. Here is what is in the sky tonight from a city balcony, and how to read it in ten minutes.

items.title: ISS pass tonight? Ask the sky over your own street
items.summary: Is there an ISS pass tonight, and what else is up? How Space Radar's Tonight view works out the sky from a named street, and what “visible” really means.

items.title: A live satellite map that tells you when it is guessing
items.summary: Space Radar is a free, open-source live satellite map of everything in orbit. Why a map of space has to be honest and kind at once, and what that costs.

items.title: How accurate is satellite tracking? Follow the numbers
items.summary: How accurate is satellite tracking, and where does the data come from? One number on Space Radar, followed back to its source, and how to correct it.

items.title: Where Is Voyager 1 Now? The Farthest Things We Threw
items.summary: Where is Voyager 1 now? One light-day from Earth, still answering on 23 watts. With Voyager 2, New Horizons, Webb and a car: what distance really means.

items.title: Where is the ISS right now? Two addresses in the sky
items.summary: Where is the ISS right now, who is aboard, and how do you see it tonight? The two places where people live in space, and what happens after 2030.

items.title: How many satellites are in orbit? The junkyard above us
items.summary: How many satellites are in orbit in 2026, how much of it is space debris, who tracks it all, and why a crash 800 km up could spoil your weather forecast.

items.title: What do satellites do? The machines you used before breakfast
items.summary: What do satellites do for you every day? How GPS really works, where the forecast comes from, and how fragile the machines behind a normal morning are.

items.title: Solar Eclipse 2027: Six Minutes of Night at Noon
items.summary: The total solar eclipse of 2 August 2027 crosses Spain, North Africa and Arabia, with six minutes of night near Luxor. Where to stand and what you’ll see.
